_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- North Carolina rule seed, 2026-08-25. Loaded
through add_rule. Holiday calendars are in
sql/sairnlaw_deadline_calendars_northcarolina.json and must be loaded too, or
every row below refuses with NOT_PROVISIONED.
NORTH CAROLINA WAS CHOSEN PARTLY BECAUSE OF WHERE ITS RULES LIVE. Its Rules of
Civil Procedure are STATUTES -- G.S. 1A-1 -- published free and in full by the
General Assembly at ncleg.gov. Kentucky was attempted first and abandoned
because the Kentucky Court of Justice does not publish its civil rules at all,
pointing instead to a commercial publisher; see
docs/sairnlaw-kentucky-deadline-seed-blockers.md. Rules 5, 6, 12, 33, 34 and 36
and G.S. 103-4 were read verbatim from ncleg.gov on 2026-08-25.
== THE CALENDAR IS A CLOSURE SCHEDULE, NOT G.S. 103-4 =====================
Rule 6(a) rolls off "a Saturday, Sunday or a legal holiday WHEN THE COURTHOUSE
IS CLOSED FOR TRANSACTIONS". It never cites G.S. 103-4, and the qualifier makes
actual closure the test. G.S. 103-4 declares about nine further days the
Judicial Branch does not close for -- Robert E. Lee's Birthday, Greek
Independence Day, the Halifax Resolves anniversary, Confederate Memorial Day,
the Mecklenburg Declaration anniversary, Washington's Birthday, First
Responders Day, Columbus Day, Yom Kippur and general election day -- and every
one would roll a deadline LATER than the truth. Full reasoning, and why this
INVERTS the Pennsylvania guidance in the engine header, is in the calendar's
own readme. The engine note has been amended to say the choice depends on what
the rule's own test is.
COVERAGE IS 2026-2027 ONLY, against 2026-2031 everywhere else, because NCAOC
publishes dated closure schedules about two years forward. Anything crossing
into 2028 refuses. The calendar needs re-running annually.
== THREE DISCOVERY RULES, THREE DIFFERENT DEFENDANT PERIODS ===============
Each of Rules 33, 34 and 36 gives an ordinary 30 days from service of the
discovery paper AND a longer alternative for a defendant measured from service
of process. The alternatives are NOT the same number:
Rule 33 interrogatories   30 / 45
Rule 34 production        30 / 45
Rule 36 admissions        30 / 60
Each was read off its own rule rather than carried across from the one before,
and Rule 36 is where getting it wrong would hurt most, because Rule 36 is
SELF-EXECUTING -- a row built on 45 days would concede facts fifteen days
before the defendant was ever required to answer.
Each is TWO rows, not one: a plain 30-day row for a party who is not a
defendant, and a resolve_periods later_of row for a defendant. That shape
exists because Georgia's equivalent was first encoded as an ordinary later_of
and shipped a date fifteen days early -- later_of picks the later trigger DATE
and then applies a single count, and these rules need a different count per
limb.
== NO later-of ROW CARRIES A SERVICE EXTENSION, AND THAT IS A REASON =======
Limb one of each runs from service of a paper under Rule 5, which Rule 6(e)
reaches. Limb two runs from service of the summons and complaint under Rule 4,
which it does not. The engine applies an extension to the winning RESULT
without knowing which limb won, so a blanket extension would sometimes lengthen
a Rule 4 period that 6(e) never touches. Compute it by hand where limb one
governs. Georgia's later-of row makes the same call.
"...served upon him by mail, three days shall be added to the prescribed
period." No other method is named, and Rule 5(b) authorises several: the
court's electronic filing system, email to an address of record, confirmed
telefacsimile, hand delivery. NONE of them extends. Three states seeded in two
days answer this three different ways -- Kentucky's eFiling Rules 13(6)
expressly treats e-service the same as mail, West Virginia's 6(e) is contested
on its own face and is refused in code, North Carolina's simply does not cover
it -- so nothing here generalises.
Sequencing is PERIOD-LENGTHENING ("added to the prescribed period"), read up
front rather than caught by a failing test.
BACKWARD PERIODS. Rule 6(d) requires a written motion and notice of hearing
"not later than five days before the time specified for the hearing" and an
opposing affidavit "at least two days before the hearing", and Rule 5(a1)
requires certain briefs "at least two days before the hearing". None is seeded,
because Rule 6(a) defines the rollover only for "the last day of the period"
running "until the end of the next day" -- forward -- and says nothing about a
period counted BEFORE an event. Rolling one in either direction would be a
guess. Three jurisdictions give three different answers to that question
(W. Va. R. Civ. P. 6(a)(5) rolls backward, Fla. 2.514(a)(5) rolls backward,
KRS 446.030(1)(b) rolls FORWARD), so there is no default to borrow. The two-day
rules additionally carry their own service definition -- actual receipt, not
ordinary service -- which this engine does not model.
APPELLATE. No North Carolina appellate row is seeded in this pass. The N.C.
Rules of Appellate Procedure are court rules rather than statutes and are not
on ncleg.gov, so they need their own source check before anything is encoded --
the gate that Kentucky taught us to run first.
RULE 6(f), the Address Confidentiality Program extension: FIVE days rather than
three, but only on "a prescribed period of 10 days or less". That is an amount
conditioned on the length of the BASE PERIOD, and amount(method) is handed only
the method. No seeded row is 10 days or shorter so it is unreachable here, and
the omission fails EARLY (three days instead of five). It must be implemented
before any short North Carolina row is added.
== EFFECTIVE_FROM IS THE ORIGINAL 1970 DATE, AND THAT IS A KNOWN WEAKNESS ==
G.S. 1A-1 took effect 1 January 1970. Individual rules have been amended since
amendment dates were NOT traced per rule for this seed. Every row therefore
claims to be in force from 1970, which is too early for any provision added
later -- a period running from a 1990s trigger would select a row whose current
text may not have applied then. Nothing in the app computes historical
deadlines today, and the calendars only cover 2026-2027 so any such request
refuses on the calendar first. Trace the amendment history before that changes.

rules.label: Answer to a complaint after service of the summons and complaint (North Carolina)

authority.quote: A defendant shall serve his answer within 30 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, not the federal 21 and not Kentucky's 20 next door. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, reached by Rule 5's scope rather than by a carve-out phrase. Rule 6(e) adds days only where a period runs "after the service of a notice or other paper", and Rule 5(b1) excepts "pleadings and papers whose service is governed by Rule 4" -- the summons and complaint go out under Rule 4. Same route as West Virginia; Georgia reaches it by express words ("other than process"), Texas and New York by inference. Rule 12(a)(1)'s closing words, "unless a different time is fixed by order of the court", attach to the motion-altered periods that follow; a court order displacing this period is in any case something the engine cannot see.

authority.quote: A party served with a pleading stating a crossclaim against him shall serve an answer thereto within 30 days after service upon him.
authority.note: The extension applies here where it does not on the answer to the complaint: a crossclaim is served under Rule 5, not Rule 4. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail. NOTE RULE 12(a)(1) NAMES NO PERIOD FOR AN ANSWER TO A COUNTERCLAIM AS SUCH -- it sets a period for the plaintiff's REPLY to a counterclaim, which is its own row. Do not use this crossclaim row for a counterclaim.

rules.label: Reply to a counterclaim contained in an answer (North Carolina)

authority.quote: The plaintiff shall serve his reply to a counterclaim in the answer within 30 days after service of the answer
authority.note: Runs from service of THE ANSWER, not from service of the counterclaim as a separate paper -- the counterclaim is in the answer. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Reply to a counterclaim where the court orders a reply (North Carolina)

authority.quote: or, if a reply is ordered by the court, within 30 days after service of the order, unless the order otherwise directs
authority.note: "UNLESS THE ORDER OTHERWISE DIRECTS" is a displacement the engine cannot see: if the order setting the reply fixes its own period, that period governs and this row's 30 days is simply wrong. Read the order before relying on this date. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Responsive pleading after the court rules on or postpones a Rule 12 motion (North Carolina)

authority.quote: The responsive pleading shall be served within 20 days after notice of the court's action in ruling on the motion or postponing its disposition until the trial on the merits;
authority.note: TWENTY DAYS, where the parent answer period is thirty -- the two halves of North Carolina's Rule 12(a) do not share a number, and neither matches the federal 21/14 pair. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: Rule 6(e) extends a period run after the SERVICE of a notice or paper, and this one runs after NOTICE OF THE COURT'S ACTION, which is not a party serving a paper under Rule 5. The subsection is also expressly subject to "unless a different time is fixed by order of the court".

rules.label: Responsive pleading after service of a more definite statement (North Carolina)

authority.quote: If the court grants a motion for a more definite statement, the responsive pleading shall be served within 20 days after service of the more definite statement.
authority.note: Runs from SERVICE of the more definite statement, so unlike its sibling in (a)(1)a the extension does reach it. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Answer after remand from a United States district court (North Carolina)

authority.quote: shall have 30 days after the filing in such State court of a certified copy of the order of remand to file motions and to answer or otherwise plead
authority.note: Runs from the FILING of the certified copy in the State court -- not from the federal court's order, not from service on anyone, and not from receipt. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: nothing is served, so Rule 6(e) has nothing to attach to. The trigger is a docket event the caller has to look up, and the engine neither derives nor validates it.

rules.label: Answers and objections to interrogatories, party other than a defendant (North Carolina)

authority.quote: The party upon whom the interrogatories have been served shall serve a copy of the answers, and objections if any, within 30 days after the service of the interrogatories.
authority.note: THIS ROW IS THE NON-DEFENDANT LIMB ONLY. Rule 33(a) continues "except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon the defendant", which is a genuine later-of and is its own resolve_periods row. Using this row for a defendant gives a date that can be far too early. "The court may allow a shorter or longer time" is a displacement the engine cannot see. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Answers and objections to interrogatories served on a defendant (North Carolina)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the interrogatories
45 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: within 30 days after the service of the interrogatories, except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon the defendant
authority.note: TWO PERIODS OF DIFFERENT LENGTHS, so this is resolve_periods and not an ordinary later_of -- the limb that wins needs its OWN count, and resolving between trigger dates first and then applying one count is how the Georgia equivalent shipped a date fifteen days early. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, and this is a REASON rather than an omission: limb one runs from service of a paper under Rule 5, which Rule 6(e) reaches, but limb two runs from service of the summons and complaint under Rule 4, which it does not. The engine applies an extension to the winning RESULT without knowing which limb won, so adding three mail days here would sometimes extend a Rule 4 period that 6(e) never touches. Same call Georgia's later-of row makes. Compute the mail extension by hand if limb one governs.

rules.label: Response to a request for production or inspection, party other than a defendant (North Carolina)

authority.quote: The party upon whom the request is served shall serve a written response within 30 days after the service of the request
authority.note: NON-DEFENDANT LIMB ONLY, exactly as with Rule 33 -- the defendant's 45-day alternative is a separate resolve_periods row. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Response to a request for production served on a defendant (North Carolina)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
45 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: within 30 days after the service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant
authority.note: Same shape and the same 30/45 numbers as the Rule 33 defendant row, and they were verified separately rather than assumed to match -- Rule 36's equivalent is 30/60, not 30/45, so within one state the three discovery rules do NOT share a second period. No service extension, for the reason given on the Rule 33 later-of row.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission, party other than a defendant (North Carolina)

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless, within 30 days after service of the request, or within such shorter or longer time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves upon the party requesting the admission a written answer or objection addressed to the matter
authority.note: SELF-EXECUTING: missing this date admits the matter, so a date computed too late here does not merely lose a filing, it concedes a fact. NON-DEFENDANT LIMB ONLY -- the defendant's 60-day floor is its own row, and note it is SIXTY here where Rules 33 and 34 use forty-five. applies_when is MAIL AND ONLY MAIL, because Rule 6(e) names no other method. North Carolina's Rule 5(b) authorises service through the court's electronic filing system, by email to an address of record, and by confirmed telefacsimile, and 6(e) reaches none of them. Do not widen this by analogy to Kentucky, whose eFiling Rules 13(6) expressly treats electronic service the same as mail.

rules.label: Answer or objection to a request for admission served on a defendant (North Carolina)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
60 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: but, unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 60 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him
authority.note: SIXTY DAYS ON LIMB TWO, NOT FORTY-FIVE. Rules 33 and 34 both give a defendant 45 days from service of process and Rule 36 gives 60, in the same statute, and the difference was read off each rule separately rather than carried across. Getting it wrong here is the worst case in the North Carolina set, because Rule 36 is self-executing: a row computed on 45 days would concede facts fifteen days before the defendant was ever required to answer. The limb is phrased as a floor -- "shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 60 days" -- which is the later-of that resolve_periods expresses. No service extension, for the reason given on the Rule 33 later-of row.
